Effect of the optical basicity on density with different Si02 content at 1823K was shown in Figure 5. The results indicted that the optical basicity has great influence on density. The trend that density changes with the optical basicity in the slag was the same as the trend that 

density changes with the mass ratio of CaO/Al2C>3. The density also decreases with the optical basicity increasing. Slags mainly are composed by the cations and complex anions, the attraction force between ions directly affect the slag density [17]. The tendency of the density changed with composition is due to the degree of polymerization, and the optical basicity may be considered to provide an alternative measure of the degree of polymerization, which is the primary factor affecting most physical properties. In molten slag system, the gradual addition of cations, e.g. Ca<sup>2+</sup> , Mg<sup>2+</sup> , results in the progressive breaking of these oxygen bonds with the formation of non-bridging oxygen (NBO), with increasing the value of optical basicity, the complex polymers of silicate complicated structures as Si044" and AIO4<sup>5</sup> " tetrahedral break down into smaller units, attraction force between ions decrease, and the density of the slag decreased. 

The structural role of A1203 in melt is also an important factor on the density. In general, when the mole ratio Al203/MO < 1 (MO: basic oxide, such as CaO, MgO), A1203 was treated as an acidic oxide [18]. However, the high CaO and AI2O3 contents with low silica in the present slag suggest that the predominant bonding would be between the two, which may lead to the changes of the existing conception in silicate melt. Future work is needed for a more systematic investigation. 

###### **Estimated Density of The Selected Limited Homogenous Phase Region** 

It is necessary to have access to reliable models for estimating density of slags, because the inherent problems and difficulties

associated with measurements at high temperature. There are many kinds of model [19] for estimating density of slag, which are physical model and semi-empirical model. Among the semi-empirical model, the geometrical model is the most attractive one, for it can estimate the properties of the high order systems with that of its sub-binary systems, without needing any information of high order systems. There are many types of geometric models available in the literature [20]. It should pointed out that the geometrical model was used only to the calculate phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties for systems when all subsystems information is known. However, it is difficult to use these models in a system with a limited homogenous phase region since its subsystem information is not available. As shown in Figure 6, the boundary of isothermal sections with a homogenous phase region does not intersect with any side of the compositional triangle and forms an island of homogenous phase region instead. In order to overcome this problem, a new model, which is the so-called the mass triangle model, is proposed by Chou [21]. Detailed discussions about this method can be found in reference. This model can use the limited data on the boundary of the homogenous region to calculate the properties within it. The advantage of this model is its flexibility to use limited experimental data within the homogenous phase region to predict the physical chemical properties at any point within the region. It has earlier been proved that the mass triangle model had been successfully used to calculation of properties in the system with a limited solubility area [22-24]. As shown in Figure 7, The selected area of CaO-5%MgO-Al203-Si02 slag in the present work has a limited homogenous phase region of liquid phase at 1823K, which the liquidus isotherms was predicated by FACTSAGE software. Based on the experimental data within this region, the mass triangle model is used to calculate density with only density information on the boundary of the homogenous phase region. Five density contour lines were calculated and shown in as open points in Figure 7. The experimental data are also shown in the same Figure as markers. It can be seen from this Figure that the calculated density agrees with the experimental data in the limited solubility area. And the present work reflected that the density decreases with the mass ratio of CaO/Al203 increasing at the same levels of SiЫ2 content which is mentioned above. Thus, the overall trend that the effects of component content on the density is in agreement with the experimental observation. ###### **Conclusions** 

(1). The densities of CaO-5%MgO-Al203-SiC>2 slag with low silica were measured by the Archimedean method in the temperature range from 1723K to 1823K. The density was found to decrease approximately linearly with an increasing temperature, as expect. 

(2). The effects of the mass ratio of CaO/Al2C>3 and optical basicity with different SiC>2 content at 1823K were investigated. The results indicated that both the mass ratio of CaO/Al2C>3 and the optical basicity had influence on the density of slag. The results demonstrated that the density decrease with the mass ratio of CaO/Al203 increasing. The trend that density changes with the optical basicity in the slag was the same as the trend that density changes with the mass ratio of CaO/Al2C>3. 

(3). Density of the selected limited homogenous phase region of CaO-5%MgO-Al203-SiC>2 slag with low silica was calculated. And the mass triangle model is working well.

Key Words: Oolimic Hematite, Magnetic Roasting, dynamics, Additive, Magnetic Susceptibility ###### **Abstract** The dynamics of oolitic hematite magnetic roasting was studied. The results show that oolitic hematite magnetic roasting was controlled by the internal diffusion, and the diffusion coefficient was 9.018xl0"7 m2 -s_1 when the oolitic hematite was roasted at 650°C. Magnetic susceptibility improves when temperature increases and roasted time prolonges under the condition of roasting at 650°Cfor 50min, with the magnetic susceptibility is 39.88%. CaF2 and Na2CC>3 can significantly improve the magnetic susceptibility at the same roasting condition, and the magnetic susceptibility was 63.35% and 57.99% respectively, thus the reduction of oolimic hematite was promoted. ###### **Introduction** With the continual depletion of free-milling iron ores and its rising price, developing the abundant resources of oolitic hematite has become one of the main research areas. The oolitic hematite accounts for 10% of China's iron ore reserve, and it also accounts for 30% of red ore reserve in China [1]. In order to exploit the oolitic hematite, there are many beneficiation research methods, including fine grinding/selective flocculation/high intensity magnetic separation or flotation, high-gradient magnetic separation, low intensity magnetic separation/high intensity magnetic separation/reverse flotation, chloridizing roasting/acid pickling, magnetic roasting/leaching process etc [2]. However, the oolitic hematite is easy to slim and the valuable mineral is covered by the slim, because of the tiny granule of value mineral, then the ooides are formed due to the state of layer morphology formed by iron ore and ganaue minerals [3, 4]. Fairly good separation indexes were hard to be obtained by traditional separation due to its structural features, so the magnetic property of the iron minerals will be changed with the use of the magnetic roasting [5, 6], which result in hematite variably altered to magnetite and simplified technological process so that a good separation indexes will be obtained by using the low intensity magnetic separation. ###### **Conclusion** 

The reaction rate is high of the oolitic hematite magnetic roasting reduction, so the rate of reduction degree is big and it can achieve high degree of reduction. The reaction is controlled by the chemical control in a relatively period when the temperature between 650°C-800°C, however, the reaction is controlled by the internal diffusion with the prolongation of the time, and the activation energy of the reaction is 14.816KJ/mol. 

The effect of the additive on diffusion coefficient is not significant, Na2S04 and Na2B407 can slightly reduce the diffusion coefficient, however, CaF2 and Na2C03 can slightly improve the diffusion coefficient. 

The magnetic susceptibility increase with the increase of temperature and time prolong, Na2S04 and Na2B407 can dramatic lower the magnetic susceptibility, however, CaF2 and Na2C03 can significantly improve the magnetic susceptibility at the same condition.

Alberto Nogueira , Cyro Takano , Marcelo Mourдo , Adolfo Pillihuaman 

Department of Metallurgical and Materials Engineering, University of Sдo Paulo, Brazil 2463 Av Prof Mello Moraes; Sдo Paulo, SP, BRAZIL Department of Metallurgical Engineering, Pontifical Catholic University of Peru 

Keywords: Self-reducing, Nuggets, Iron Ore, Slag, Rotary Kiln, Coalescence. 

###### **Abstract*

* 

The self-reduction is an alternative and promising process for production of pig iron because offers decisive benefits such as enhancing the reaction kinetic with decrease in fuel consumption and CO2 emissions. The self-reduction mixture of iron ore fines, carbonaceous reducer and additives for slag forming components, without agglomeration, was tested in a laboratory rotary kiln. The additives for slag were defined for presenting two different estimated _liquidus_ temperatures (1623 K and 1773 K) to verify the effect of these temperatures on the iron-carbon nuggets coalescence process. These mixtures were tested at 1673 and 1773 K in an experimental rotary kiln. After reduction-melting and coalescence processes the samples were disaggregated and the iron nuggets were classified by size. It was considered that nuggets larger than 7,93mm would be a good reference for coalescence index. Low _liquidus_ temperature slag presented 37% of this larger fraction against only 13.5% for high _liquidus_ temperature one. The low _liquidus_ temperature slag would facilitate contact between the particles of iron-carbon in a rotary kiln, enhancing the coalescence. 

###### **Introduction** 

The slag composition usually depends on the reducer ash composition, the ore gangue, the binder composition and any fluxing material [1], and the mechanism of carbon transportation in slag that contains iron oxide reducible by carbon can be explained by the oxide reduction and the metal carburization. During carbon transportation, the carburized particle is transported to slagmetal interphases by the gravity effect, being assimilated by the metallic phase [2]. When the slag's iron oxide comes in contact with the solid carbon, it is immediately reduced, forming Fe particles and CO bubbles as it is shown in the figure 1(a). The Fe particles are carburized by carbon particles; they are liquefied simultaneously in the carbon-slag interphase. The Fe-C liquid particles are transported from the slag-carbon interphase to iron-slag interphase as a result of slag flow, based on the surface tension difference _(Marangoni_ effect), figure 1(b). The Fe-C liquid particles coalesce on the iron surface and the carbon is immediately diffused in the iron as it is shown in figure 1 (c). The reduced iron is carburized continuously by repeated sequences [3]. 

117 



Figure 1. The carburation's process - _Marangoni_ effect [3]. 

What is usually called as a carburized slag is an emulsion of silicate slag and molten carbide, the last one contains a considerable dissolved oxide's amount. The slag as an ionic liquid contains dissolved carbon, which could be in the form of anion carbide (C2" slag reducer) or carbonate (CO3" slag oxidant), and then, it is generated the concept of slag's carbide capacity. The dissolved carbides inside the slag are capable of carburizing metals that are in contact with them at high temperatures [4, 5]. 

In normal conditions, the carbon has low solubility in slag,

therefore the carbon needs transportation's mean to be transported through the slag, which could be supplied by an oxide reducer. Several studies showed indirectly that when slag lacks reducer oxide, or worse, it does not reach the _liquidus_ temperature, the tendency will be a carburization's prevention, acting as a physical barrier as it is shown in figure 2 [6]. • c O

###### EFFECT OF MIXED CHARGE OF ORE AND LUMP COAL ON THE SOFTENING-MELTING PROPERTY OF THE BURDEN 

Guo Hongwei Yang Guangqing* Zhang Jianliang Shao Jiugang Fu Yuandi Wan Dan 

School of Metallurgical and Ecological Engineering, University of Science and Technology Beijing; 

30 Xueyuan Road, Haidian District, Beijing, 100083, P.R.China 

**Keywords:** Blast furnace, Lump coal, Softening-melting Property 

###### **Abstract** 

Resource of metallurgical coke is becoming scarce, and although coke can be partially replaced by pulverized coal injection, there are many restrictions for further increase in coal ratio. Mixed charge of ore and lump coal from top to replace more coke was studied in this paper. Softening-melting property of the burden was affected by charge of lump coal. Softening-melting properties of mixed charge of ore and coke, mixed charge of ore and lump coal were tested respectively. Results show: the property of the burden mixed with coke is superior to the burden mixed with lump coal; lump coal would not deteriorate softening-melting property of the burden and some of them can even improve softening-melting property of the burden. Top charge of lump coal would not deteriorate softening-melting process, and this should be a new way to increase coal consumption to decrease coke rate. 

###### **Introduction** 

The blast furnace is still the predominant process for the reduction of iron ore and will probably remain so for the next decades. Metallurgical coke is becoming scarce and expensive, so the cost of hot metal can be decreased by reducing the consumption of metallurgical coke[l]. Coke can be partially replaced by pulverized coal injection, currently the highest rate of pulverized coal reached 266kg/tHM, most of blast furnace PCR is about 150kg/tHM, and it is very difficult to further increase of PCR. Nut coke is charged into blast furnace mixed with iron ore, not only for improving util

ization of metallurgical coke, but also for lowering the coke rate. Presently the majority of blast furnaces in the world use nut coke although its amount is very different: from 10-20 to 70-100 kg/tHM and more[2-4].The effect of nut coke in blast furnace is extensively researched, and the main conclusions recommend: to improve

gas permeability of cohesive layer in blast furnace, to promote reduction of iron burden, protect metallurgical coke from the solution in the shaft due to higher reactivity of nut coke. There is no special requirement for the strength of nut coke[5-8]. Nut coke is also used for sintering fuel, which may lead to the shortage of the nut coke charging into blast furnace. So lump coal mixed with iron ore is considered to be charged into the blast furnace, not only to reduce the cost of grinding coal, but also to increase the use amount of coal. 

Little research has been done on the effect of lump coal on the smelting process of blast furnace. The softening-melting property of the lump coal and iron ore mixture, the coke and iron ore mixture, iron ore are studied in this paper, and the results obtained are compared and analyzed.

###### EFFECTS OF OXYGEN CONTENT AND ROASTING TEMPERATURE ON THE SINTERING MINERALIZATION PROPERTIES OF DIFFERENT IRON ORES 

Xiaoming Mao, Zhixiong You , Yuanbo Zhang, Zhenyu Fan, Tao Jiang 

(School of Minerals Processing & Bioengineering, Central South University, Changsha, 

Hunan 410083, China) 

Key Words: sintering, mineralization, iron ore, calcium ferrite 

###### **Abstract** 

It is generally known that the formation of calcium ferrite is favorable during the iron ore sintering, which dominatingly contributes to the improvement of strength and reducibility of the finished sinters. In this study, effects of roasting temperature and 0 2 content of inlet gas on the sintering mineralization properties of typical iron ores, including hematite, limonite, spйculante and magnetite, were investigated. The results showed the amount of calcium ferrite initially increased then decreased with the increase of the roasting temperature. The temperature of maximum calcium ferrite generation amount for different iron ores was determined as follows: hematite and limonite was 1275 °C, whereas specularite and magnetite was 1250 °C. Increasing 0 2 content of inlet gas was advantageous to the generation of calcium ferrite during the sintering. The sequence of 0 2 content affecting the mineralization properties of different iron ores was determined as follows: magnetite > hematite > specularite > limonite. 

###### **Introduction** 

The mineralization property of iron ore plays a significant role in the mineral composition and microstructure of finished sinters, which determine the quality and output of the sinters [1-2]. The mineralization process of sinters is composed of solid-phase reaction, formation of liquid-phase and crystallization. The formation and crystallization of liquid-phase is the foundation to the mineralization as the quality of the sinter is poor when concreted by solid-phase consolidation [3-4]. With respect to the iron ore sintering, liquid-phase regarded as bonding phase is generated between the iron ores and fluxes at high temperature [5]. Calcium ferrite is the most favorable liquid-phase among the bonding phases which dominatingly contributes to the improvement of strength and reducibility of the finished sinters [6-8]. Especially for high iron-low silicon sintering and high basicity sintering, making sure sufficient calcium ferrite quantity and reasonable distribution is crucial to the

sinters [9-10]. Therefore, carrying out the

researches on the high temperature reaction properties of iron ores is of great significance [11]. 

On the other hand, components of inlet gas exert vital impacts on the iron ore sintering properties. It is widely accepted that oxidizing atmosphere is essential condition for the formation of calcium ferrite as the conventional sintering process is considered as an oxidization sintering. The sintering indexes would become worse when O2 content in the inlet gas reduces, moreover, the combustion of coke breeze and oxidation of FeO will be affected tremendously [12]. 

In this study, effects of roasting temperature and O2 content of the inlet gas on the mineralization properties of different types of iron ores were systematically investigated by means of a micro-sintering method.

###### Methods 

First, iron ore fines and calcium oxide (CaO) were ground to 100% passing through 0.074 mm. Then , the ground iron ores and CaO were dried in air-oven at 120 °C for 8 h and mixed thoroughly with a certain proportion. To make sure the maximum generation of calcium ferrite, the basicity and moisture of the mixture were determined as 3.0 and 10%, respectively. 2.0 g mixture was weighed and agglomerated to be a cylindric briquette with 10 mm in diameter under the pressure of 10 MPa. 

After that, the briquette was dried in air and put in a corundum porcelain boat, then roasted at the micro-sintering device, which was plotted in Figure 1. The composition of inlet gas was controlled by adjusting the flowmeters of gas cylinders and analyzed after mixed in a buffer

After roasted at given temperature for certain period, cooling procedure was carried out along the opposite direction at the same speed. The roasting time and flow velocity of inlet gas were fixed at 5 min and 5.0 L/min, respectively. Roasting temperature varied from 1200-1325 °C. 

The microstructure of roasted briquettes was stud

###### Microstructure Of Roasted Magnetite Briquettes 

The effects of O2 content on the sintering mineralization properties of magnetite were remarkable. In fact, O2 content firstly affected the oxidation of magnetite and then the generation of calcium ferrite. In this study, microstructure of magnetite briquettes roasted at different oxygen content varying from 8% to 21% was investigated using an optical microscope. The roasting temperature was kept at 1275 °C. The microstructural photos were displayed in Figure 7. 



A(0 2 8%) 

136 



Shiny white and light grey exhibited in Figure 7 represented magnetite and calcium ferrite, respectively. Magnetite was easily oxidized to hematite in the oxidizing atmosphere at 1275 °C, which firstly appeared at the edge of magnetite particles. It was observed that calcium ferrite was unequally distributed. A skeleton framework was formed as magnetite was oxidized insufficiently and crystalline grain was imperfectly developed in micrographs A, B and C. The quality of the roasted sinters and generation amount of calcium ferrite was unsatisfactory under these conditions. When the oxygen content of inlet gas is relatively lower, there were more unoxidized magnetite particles remained in the roasted briquettes (micrographs A and B). The zone of light grey from the micrograph A to E expanded as more magnetite particles were oxidized to hematite, and then they could react with calcium oxide to form calcium ferrite, when O2 content of inlet gas was increased. Calcium ferrite, existing in the micrographs D and E, was well crystallized and connected with each other, exhibiting tabular or massive structure, which was beneficial for the strength of the finished sinters. The research results further showed that the oxygen content of inlet gas was very important for the sintering of magnetite. During the sintering, magnetite must be quickly oxidized completely. Otherwise, the generation amount of calcium ferrite is limited, which is seriously disadvantageous to the quality of the finished sinters. 

###### **Conclusions** 

[1] The generation amount of calcium ferrite first increased then decreased with the roasting temperature ascending. The suitable temperatures at which the maximum amount of calcium ferrite was generated for different types of iron ores were measured as follows: hematite and limonite was 1275 °C, and specularite and magnetite was 1250 °C. The corresponding maximum generation amount of calcium ferrite was 73.14%, 97.13%, 67.47% and 62.88%, respectively. 

[2] Increasing O2 content of inlet gas was advantageous to the generation of calcium ferrite, which exhibited a growing trend with the increase of oxygen content of inlet gas. The sequence of 0 2 content affecting on the mineralization properties of different iron ores was measured as follows: magnetite > hematite > specularite > limonite. 

[3] 0 2 content played a significant role

in improving the microstructure and quality of the sinters when using magnetite as materials. When the oxygen content of inlet gas is relatively lower, there were more unoxidized magnetite particles remained in the roasted briquettes.

###### HOT WORKABILITY OF M42 TOOL STEEL ADDITIONALLY ALLOYED WITH CO AND MO 

Milan Tercelj<sup>1</sup> , Goran Kugler<sup>1</sup> , Matevz Fazarinc<sup>1</sup> , IztokPerus<sup>1</sup> 

'University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Natural Sciences and Engineering; Askerceva 12, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia, Europe 

Keywords: hot deformation behavior, AISI M42 tool steel, carbide precipitation 

###### **Abstract** 

Hot deformability of M42 tool steel additionally alloyed with cobalt and molybdenum was investigated. Hot-compression tests were carried out in the temperature range 850 °C - 1200 °C, at strain rates range 0.001-6s-l up to strain of 0.9. Field-emission scanning electron microscope and optical microscopy were used for characterization of microstructure of deformed samples, which revealed a very complex precipitation of carbides that strongly depends on the soaking temperature, the soaking time, the stress state, the deformation temperature as well as on the strain rate. Gathered data was used to calculate the processing parameters such as process maps, apparent activation energies and strain hardening exponents. For better understanding of thermodynamical properties of the studied steel a simultaneous thermal analysis was conducted. Furthermore the analysis of phase equilibrium was calculated using Thermo-Calc software. On the basis of these studies the optimal soaking temperature and process windows were determined. 

###### **Introduction** 

Hot workability of ledeburitic tool steels is important economic factor. This means that for each tool steel individuallysafe range of hot working parameters should be revealed. Publications in the literature with regard to the hot workability of tool steels are rare and therefore more informat

ion from this research area is desired.The relatively low hot workability of ledeburitic tool steels, i.e. steels in which the solidification is completed by a eutectic transformation of the residual interdendritic liquid to austenite and various alloy carbides (ledeburitic carbides), is usually characterized by the production of surface and internal cracks during the hot deformation. 

Tool steels are highly alloyed with Cr, W, Mo, V, etc., i.e. carbide forming elements which essentially influence hot workability. The following types of carbides are usually present in microstructure: MC, M2C, M6C, M7C3, and M23C6, [1]. During heating, soaking and hot deformation, various processes regarding the carbides take place in the steel, i.e. decomposition, dissolution, formation as well as their growth and coarsening. The type of carbides, their quantity, morphology, shape and size depend on the chemical composition of steel and processing parameters, e.g. casting temperature, solidification rate, soaking temperature and time.The upper limit of the temperature working range is related so to occurrence of incipient melting of eutectics (carbides) and phases with low melting point on grain boundaries as well as to grain growth, [2]. On other hand lower limit of safe hot working range is related to precipitation of secondary carbides, characteristics of primary carbides in the matrix and/or on 

147 

grain boundaries as well as to decreased recrystallization rate [3]. Slightly variations in so in process parameters as well as in chemical composition can shift so upper as well as lower limit of temperature working range; consequently it is very important to reveal process windows of safe hot working for wide range of microstructure states for each studied steel, [4-10]. 

For achieving of desired mechanical properties of standard tool steels beside carbide-forming also other chemical elements can be added that usually results in decreased hot workability. In our case hot workability of BRM02 tool steel which was additionally alloyed with Co and Mo was investigated.For this purpose hot compression tests in wide range of deformation conditions were carried out for two states of steel; first batch of samples was gathered after initial casting from the ingot head, while the other batch was taken from an 18 mm rod. This served as a comparison of the two states, for which processing maps, thermo-mechanical parameters and ThermoCalc analysis were made. 

###### **Experimental Procedure** 

For evaluation of thermo-mechanical responses of the tested steel, compression tests were conducted on specimens machined from cast and wrought ingots of AISI M42 tool steel. 

The compression tests were conducted on the thermo-mechanical simulator Gleeble 1500D in a protective atmosphere, with strain rates ranging from 0.001 s"<sup>1</sup> to 5 s"<sup>1</sup> and temperatures between 850 °C and 1130 °C or 1150 °C, for cast and wrought state, respectively. The samples were first

heated to austenitization temperature with 4 K/s, where they were held for 10 minutes prior to cooling to deformation temperature with 6 K/s where they were held for 10 min prior to deformation. Right after deformation the samples were submerged in water. Austenitization temperature was selected on a basis of series of compression test, where it was selected as the highest temperature at which after deforming the samples to strain of 0.9 with a strain rate of 1 s"1 no macro cracks were present on the surface of the specimens [11-15]. True stress vs. logarithmic straincurves were calculated, taking intoaccount the heat generated due to thehigh strain rates. The temperature risewas compensated for by applying themethod proposed by Liu et al[16]. The deformed specimens were cutalong the mid-plane and metallographicallyprepared by grinding, polishingand etching in Vilella's reagent. Lightoptical microscopy was used to observethe microstructural features ineach sample. ###### **Results and Discussions** ###### Stress-strain Curves The data, gathered from the stress/strain curves shows, that the stresses, needed for plastic deformation of wrought stare are about 10-15 % greater than those needed for deformation of ascast state (Figure 1). This can be contributed to a variety of different factors, all leading to the increase of flow stresses. First and foremost factor is the mechanical dispersion of carbides throughout the matrix, which cause the barrier for grain growth and harden the matrix. This 148 effect can be clearly seen form the Figure 2a where spheroidized eutectic carbides can be seen. There are also secondary carbides present in the austenitic grains (Figure 2b). They were calculated for both cast and wrought state (Figure 4). The instability regions could only be observed in the maps calculated for cast state, whereas for the wrought state no instability regions occurred. The instability regions are closely related to deformation capabilities of material. The cast steel consists of large austenitic grains, trapped inside a carbide matrix, which is tough and fragile and brakes under tensile stress. To safely deform this kind of material, a hydrostatic pressure state has to be present in material during hot deformation. This is usually achieved during hot forging process. When the carbide network is sufficiently broken into smaller and rounder carbides, hot rolling could also be used for deformation of the material. The intergranular cracking could be observed in the Figure3. The micrograph was taken on the edge of the sample, deformed in the region, where the instability was calculated (strain rate of 0.1 s"1 and temperature of 1130 °C). The presented micrograph clearly shows the cracking of the structure along the grain boundaries. The values of efficiency of power dissipation in the temperature region between 850 and 950 °C and between 1 and 5 s"1 are very low (~15 %) (Figure 4a). This means that only a small part of dissipated energy is used for microstructural changes, and most of it is transformed into heat. 151 ###### **Conclusions** An analysis of hot deformability of AISI M42 tool-steel was conducted on the basis of hot compression tests. The results showed that: - Stresses needed for hot deformation of wrought steel were higher than those required for deformation of cast steel. This was explained via the difference in carbide distribution in the samples. - Thermo-mechanical parameters were calculated for both states of steel, and were calculated for lower and higher temperature region. The border between the two was determined as the temperature, where MC-type carbides start to precipitate. This was determined using Thermo-Calc calculations. This was confirmed by good correlation between calculated and measured values of themo-mechanical parameters. - The calculated processing maps have shown regions of unstable material flow in the cast state, which should be avoided in the early stages of forming, especially at high temperatures and low strain rates. These regions disappear with the right selection of austenitization temperature, as can be seen from the processing maps, calculated for wrought state. - The austenitization temperature was selected using an array of special compression tests, which have shown, that the best austenitization temperature was 40-50 °C under the melting temper

ature of the carbides with the lowest melting temperature.

###### Effects of Crystallization of Mould Fluxes on Property of Liquid Slag Film and Its Impacts on Peritectic Steel Slab Continuous Casting 

Xiao Long , Shengping He , Lilong Zhu , Ting Wu , Qian Wang 'Chongqing Key Laboratory of Metallurgical Engineering, College of Materials Science and Engineering, Chongqing University, Chongqing 400044, China 

Keywords: Mould fluxes; Crystallization; Liquid slag film; Property; Peritectic steel; Continuous casting. 

###### **Abstract** 

During the continuous casting of peritectic steel slabs, mould fluxes with high crystallization capacity are usually chosen for improving slab surface quality. However, the lubrication condition of casting shell also could be deteriorated. Since precipitation of crystals within liquid slag film can change the composition and property of liquid slag over solid-liquid slag film interface region, its impacts on continuous casting process also are not clear. In order to clear this phenomenon, an experiment method was put forward, and mould fluxes for peritectic steel slabs continuous casting were selected and examined. The results reveal that after crystals have been separated, the crystallization capacity of leftover liquid slag increased with different levels, which could deteriorate the lubrication condition of casting shell and cause a series of problems. Thereby, mould fluxes with high crystallization capacity at beginning for heat tran

sfer control and then weaker after crystallization should be considered in the future. 

###### **Introduction** 

In the continuous casting of peritectic steel slabs, contradiction between heat transfer control and slab shell lubrication by mould fluxes has been treated as a key problem for maintaining a smooth manufacturing process [1]. Strong and uneven horizontal heat flux over the meniscus region will cause uneven solidification of casting shell, especially for peritectic steel slab with enormous volume change caused by phase transition. All of those could cause surface defects like longitudinal crack [2-4]. 

For normal peritectic steel slabs casting, mould fluxes with high basicity and crystallization capacity are commonly used for heat transfer control [5,6]. But the lubrication condition of casting shell could be deteriorated after casting speed was enhanced. In actual process, the composition and property of the liquid slag over the solid-liquid interfacial region will change after taking crystals out within liquid slag, and previous work has been carried out on this phenomenon [7]. But the major 

155 

method adopted in previous work to obtain the post-precipitated liquid slag was only based on calculation, and only the situation with single crystallization phase was taken into account. In actual process, crystallization phase may change in precipitation process, thus the actual composition change tendency of post-precipitated liquid slag may be different from the calculation ones. For further understanding this phenomenon, three typical peritectic steel mould fluxes were adopted and an experiment was developed to analysis the property change tendencies of remainder liquid slags after crystals have been separated out, and its impacts on casting process were also discussed.

Fracture of 2# (left) and 2#-80% (right) samples ###### Discussion Mould fluxes for peritectic steel slab continuous casting must meet the requirements of heat transfer control and lubrication. For 1# and 2# slag, especially for 1#, original slag's crystalliza

tion capacity can not meet the requirement for heat transfer control, especially for high speed casting, defects like longitudinal crack are unavoidable. But for 3# slag, the crystallization phase is cuspidine, and the Vi grade is 1. It means 3# original slag has high crystallization capacity and which can uniform the heat flux over meniscus region effectively. However the crystallization temperature and break temperature of its post-precipitated liquid slags increase obviously, this result indicates the casting process will become very unstable after the temperature fluctuation over meniscus region exceeds some degrees. May be it is just the reason why continuous casting process become so unstable when high basicity mould fluxes are adopted. From this point, the restriction of high speed continuous casting of peritectic steel slab is the property-change problem and scientific research should be performed. At the same time, the mould fluxes with high crystallization capacity at beginning for heat transfer control and then crystallization capacity become stable or even lower for lubrication after taking crystals out within liquid slag should be considered. 

###### **Conclusions** 

For traditional mould fluxes used on peritectic steel slab continuous casting, break temperature, crystallization temperature and crystallization ability of post-precipitated liquid slag increase in varying degrees after crystallization. The lubrication condition of casting shell will be deteriorated at the same time. It should be the restriction of high speed continuous casting of peritectic steel slab. Therefore the mould fluxes with high crystallization capacity at beginning for heat transfer control and weaker after crystals have been separated out for lubrication should be considered.

###### HOT DUCTILITY OF NB-V CONTAINING MICROALLOYED STEEL DURING SOLIDIFICATION 

Yanhui Sun, Yanan Zeng, Kaike Cai 

University of Science and Technology Beijing 30 Xueyuan Road, Haidian District, Beijing, 100083 P. R.China 

Keywords: Solute Segregation; High Temperature Brittle Zone; Low Strain Rate; Precipitation; Critical Stress 

###### **Abstract** 

Hot ductility of Nb-V-containing steel has been studied by theoretical calculation and thermal simulation experiment. Meanwhile, microsegregation and precipitates were analyzed. The results showed that segregation degree of elements S, P, O is greater in mushy zone, while, the hot ductility was deteriorated by inclusions of Fe(S,0), (Fe,Mn,Si,Al)(S,0) in the interdendritic region. At the temperature 1100 C, a few NbN particles, 60-70nm, have little effect on mechanical property. In the temperature range 1000 C to 975 C, R.A declined rapidly from 82.36% to 69.61% with the diameters decreasing from 20 to lOnm and quantity of particles increased 23 to 45inds/u.m<sup>2</sup> , respectively. In the temperature range from 900 C to 850 C, R.A reduced unobviously from 34.27 % to 30.01% with ferric films thickening gradually. The critical stress, 52.38MPa, was equal to tensile strength at 975 C. Intergranular fracture was easy to occur with higher critical stress below 975 C. 

###### **Introduction** 

Productivity and product quality of slab are seriously affected by cracks during continuous casting and the influencing factors of cracks are variousfl]. From microcosmic angle, resisting deformation ability of initial solidification shell decreases obviously with solute elements segregation which can urge the low melting point of liquid film to form at grain boundaries[2, 3]. Meanwhile, with temperature decreasing, particles would precipitate as the practical solubility product is greater than equilibrium solubility product. The carbonitrides would lead to stress concentration at austenite grain boundaries. Therefore, the transverse cracks of microalloyed steel would form during the straightening operation in the continuous casting process. The hot ductility of steels in the temperature of mushy zone was characterized by microalloy elements segregation, zero strength temperature (ZST) and zero ductility temperature (ZDT). The nature, shape, and size of precipitates have been investigated by TEM

(JEM2100). Hot tensile test with low strain rate was simulated by Gleeble-1500. In order to explain the fracture mechanism of microalloyed steel, the point A, B in Figure 2 (a) were analyzed by EDS. Цzlem Okur, Murat Alkan, Onuralp Yiicel

###### **Abstract** 

In this study, Co-Cr-Mo alloys were produced using a mixture of C03O4, Cr2Ы3 and M0O3 powders with Al powders by a

Self-propagating high temperature synthesis process. SHS is a process of material synthesis that has revealed a number of reactants combinations capable of much higher energy release than conventional explosives. AI2O3 is added to the mixture to decrease the adiabatic temperature of the system. The thermodynamic simulations and the calculations of adiabatic temperature were examined with FactSage 6.2. In the SHS experiments, different C03O4/ C^CVMoC^ ratios were examined, and their effects on the metal recovery and alloy compositions were carried out. The samples were characterized by using chemical analysis, XRD, XRF and SEM/EDS techniques. 

###### **Introduction** 

Self Propagating High Temperature Synthesis (SHS) has significant advantages compared to the high technology furnace applications, such as very short processing time, simple operation, low energy requirement and low cost [1,2]. In a SHS process, the ignition starts the combustion and propagates throughout the reactant mixture yielding the desired product. However, the disadvantages of the process such as inhomogeneous or unreacted products due to undesirable reaction rates needs to be overcome by changing some parameters such as ignition temperature, particle size, additive, atmosphere etc. [3, 4]. This work aims to establish a scientific and engineering background in the production of some cast Co-Cr-Mo master alloys via SHS (Self Propagating High Temperature Synthesis) metallurgy which is attractive process technique regarding fast and low-cost production ability of cast alloys. 

###### **Experimental Procedure** 

In the SHS experiments, C03O4, Cr2C>3, M0O3 and Al powders were used in order to produce CoCr-Mo master alloys. The raw materials have over 96 % purity and 200 um average grain sizes. The initial mixtures were calculated and prepared to produce alloys containing 12.5-50.0 % Co, 12.5-50.0 % Cr, 12.5-50.0 % Mo by weight. The advanced thermochemical simulations of the reactions were investigated in detail including different ratios of initial mixtures, and their effects on metal recoveries, metal distributions and alloy compositions were carried out. 

The reaction mixtures were mixed thoroughly 15 minutes in a turbula mixer and powder mixtures (approximately 150 g) were charged into Cu crucible and compacted. W (tungsten) 

171 

wire was placed at the top of copper crucible and the reaction realized by passing current through the wire. After initiation, a highly exothermic reaction became self-sustaining and propagated throughout the SHS mixture. The obtained SHS products were discharged from the crucible after cooling. The phase compositions of the SHS products were characterized by using XRD, XRF and chemical analysis (AAS) techniques.

eng, Germain Kouma Ndong, Jun Zhu, Qiaochu Liu 

School of Metallurgical and Ecological Engineering University of Science and Technology Beijing Xueyuan Road 30, 100083 Beijing, China 

Keywords: Aluminum electrolysis, inert anode, oxidation, corrosion behaviors. 

###### **Abstract** 

High-temperature oxidation and corrosion behaviors of Ni-Fe-Cr alloy as inert anodes for aluminum electrolysis have been studied in oxygen and molten electrolyte. The oxidation and corrosion scales on the anodes tested were analyzed using XRD and SEM-EDS. The oxidation rate is found to increase with increasing temperature from 700 °C to 950 °C, which can be approximately described by an inverse power rate function. The oxidation scales at 750 °C, 920 °C and 950 °C contain Cr-rich phase along with FeCr204 and (Fe0.6Cro.4)203. The corrosion extent of Ni-Fe-Cr anodes in electrolyte is dominated by temperature, which can make the scales thickness double from 700 °C to 750 °C or from 920 °C to 950 °C. Cr and Fe in the scales on the anode in electrolysis corrode preferentially into the molten electrolyte, while the nickel oxides could better sustain the corrosive environment in electrolysis. The results can be useful for developing inert anode material for potential application in aluminum electrolysis. 

###### **Introduction** 

The development of an inert anode for aluminum electrolysis has been a long term goal for aluminum industry. The present process for primary aluminum production involves the reduction of alumina with carbon anodes, forming carbon dioxide: 



The search for a suitable non-carbon anode has been done in the last few decades to significantly reduce greenhouse emissions and production costs associated with the carbon anode consumption. Using an inert anode, the primary anodic reaction is oxygen evolution: 



To withstand the highly corrosive conditions in aluminum electrolysis cell, the inert anode materials must have excellent oxidation resistance. Among the materials under consideration, NiFe-based alloys and their composite materials have shown a promise for industry application that has received great attention '' . Unfortunately, Ni-Fe alloys under oxidizing conditions develop layered corrosion scales containing Fe^O and/or other metal oxides, which may either provide 

some protection to further oxidation or result in more corrosion/erosion on the alloy anodes during aluminum electrolysis '<sup>6-</sup><sup>_7_</sup> _\_ 

_111_ 

Cu-Ni-Fe and Ni-Fe-Co ternary alloys have been studied as candidate materials system for the inert anodes. It was found that Cu-Ni-Fe alloy had a two- phase microstructure of Cu-rich phase and Fe-Ni-rich phase '<sup>8</sup> ' and such chemical non-homogeneity showed a negative impact on their corrosion resistance. This is because the Fe-rich phase can be preferentially corroded during aluminum electrolysis, thus providing iron-fluoride corrosion tunnels within the anode corrosion scales . For Ni-Fe-Co ternary allo

y, the additions of 10 wt.% and 30 wt.% Co to the Ni-Fe alloy system were found to significantly improve the anodic wear resistance and oxidation resistance due to the suppression of FexO formation. However, the reaction scales had excessive porosity, non-homogeneity and poor surface adherence, which could not provide sufficient protection to the metal anodes I<sup>10</sup> "<sup>11</sup> !. 

The present study is aimed to investigate the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of ternary Ni-FeCr alloy as well as its reaction scale in light of the requirements for inert anodes in aluminum electrolysis. In particular, the influence of temperature on the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of Ni-Fe-Cr alloy was studied in oxygen and molten electrolyte at 700 °C - 950 °C.

###### **Conclusion** 

1. The oxidation rate of the Ni-Fe-Cr anodes increases with increasing testing temperature from 700 °C through 950 °C, which can be approximately described by an inverse power rate function, but the complex reaction mechanism may need further investigation. 

2. The corrosion scales formed in oxidation at elevated temperatures (750 °C, 920 °C and 950 °C) contain Cr-rich phase (FeCr2C>4 and (Feo.6Cro.4)2C>3, etc.). 

183 

3. The corrosion extent of Ni-Fe-Cr alloy in aluminum electrolyte is dominated by temperature, and the thickness of the scales is increased double from 700°C to 750°C or from 920°C to 950°C. 

4. Cr and Fe in the scales on the alloy anode during aluminum electrolysis can corrode preferentially into the molten electrolyte, while the nickel oxides could better sustain a corrosive environment in molten electrolyte.

Dilek Kirgцz, Murat Alkan, Onuralp Yiicel

Keywords: Intermetallics, Fe-based alloys, Molybdenum, Metallothermic process 

###### **Abstract** 

In this study, Mo containing Fe-based alloys, such as Fe-Ni-Cr-Mo, were synthesized using a mixture of Fe203-NiO-Cr203-MoC>3 powders reducing with Al powders by metallothermic process which is a high energy efficient, fast and low-cost production technique for synthesis of cast alloys and advanced ceramics. Detailed thermochemical studies were simulated by using FactSage 6.2 Thermochemical software in order to calculate adiabatic temperature of the reactions and effects of initial molar composition on the final products. In the metallothermic processes, effects of stoichiometric Al addition and addition of the oxide powders (AI2O3, SiC>2, CaO, MgO) on the metal recovery and compositions of final alloys were carried out. Final products were characterized by using chemical analysis (AAS), XRD, XRF and SEM/EDS techniques. 

###### **Introduction** 

Self Propagating High Temperature Synthesis (SHS) has significant advantages compared to the high technology furnace applications, such as very short processing time, simple operation, low energy requirement and low cost [1,2]. In a SHS process, the ignition starts the combustion and propagates throughout the reactant mixture yielding the desired product. However, the disadvantages of the process such as inhomogeneous or unreacted products due to undesirable reaction rates needs to be overcome by changing some parameters such as ignition temperature, particle size, additive, atmosphere etc. [3, 4]. This work aims to establish a scientific and engineering background in the production of some cast Fe based alloys (Fe-Ni-Cr-Mo) which are used as surface coatings, wear-corrosion-oxidation resistive applications via SHS (Self Propagating High T

emperature Synthesis) metallurgy which is attractive process technique regarding fast and low-cost production ability of cast alloys. ###### **Experimental Procedure** In the SHS experiments, Fe2C>3, NiO, Cr2C>3, M0O3 and Al powders were used in order to produce Fe-Ni-Cr, and Fe-Ni-Cr-Mo alloys. The raw materials have over 96 % purity and 200 um average grain sizes. The initial mixtures were calculated and prepared to produce alloys containing 8-14% Ni, 18% Cr, 3% Mo, and balance Fe by weight. The advanced thermochemical simulations of the reactions were investigated in detail including different ratios of initial mixtures, appropriate flux, heat sinker or increaser additions as well as different initial temperatures in order to reduce the number of experiments. Due to economical reason with the 185 addition of CaO, MgO, Si02 or AI2O3 as a flux into the green mixtures 10-30% by weight, and their effects on metal recoveries, metal distributions and alloy compositions were carried out. The reaction mixtures were mixed thoroughly 15 minutes in a turbula mixer and powder mixtures (approximately 150 g) were charged into Cu crucible and compacted. W (tungsten) wire was placed at the top of copper crucible and the reaction realized by passing current through the wire. After initiation, a highly exothermic reaction became self-sustaining and propagated throughout the SHS mixture. The obtained SHS products were discharged from the crucible after cooling. The phase compositions of the SHS products were characterized by using XRD, XRF and chemical analysis (AAS) techniques. ###### **Results and Discussions** Before the SHS experiments, a thermochemical simulation was performed to estimate the effect of precursor compositions on the SHS process. In this investigation, FGM was tested for use as part of the cathode materials, where a 10 mm thick TiB2-rich layer was on the top as an Al-wettable surface, the TiB2-C layers

in the middle as a gradient layer and the carbon on the bottom as a base. Electrical resistances of FGM were determined in the temperature range of 25960°C in argon atmosphere. The results show that the present of TiB2-C gradient layer can reduce the open porosity and the electrical resistance of the cathodes materials at elevated temperatures. The cathode samples after aluminum electrolysis usually demonstrates an increase in electrical resistance, but the application of FGM layer can compensate such an increase for certain extend due to less variation in porosity and lower the level of melts penetration. 

###### **Introduction** 

Carbon is still used for aluminum reduction cathodes dominantly, but it has a poor wetting properties by liquid aluminum and the anode-cathode distance has to be kept about 4-5cm with an additional 1.3-2.0 V voltage drop [1]. TiB2 has better wettability by liquid aluminum with higher electrical conductivity and stronger chemical resistance to the electrolyte attack. And the wettability of TiB2-C composites cathode on liquid aluminum can be also improved, while liquid aluminum can completely wet the cathode surface if TiB2 content exceeds 27% [2-4]. However, during the process of TiB2-C composites cathodes preparation and aluminum electrolysis, the deformation by temperature variation or sodium penetration are great disparity between TiB2 and carbon due to their physical properties difference. This will accelerate the cathodes cracking and deterioration. 

Function Gradient Materials (FGM) is a novel materials with components, microstructures and properties changed in gradient, which can ease the strain and stress caused by the properties difference between different materials. These may relieve the problems in carbon cathodes contained TiB2 and bring well performances beyond a simply TiB2-C composites cathode. In our previous works, TiB2-C/C FGM cathode has been designed and prepared in laboratory, and the sodium expansion has been test by modified Rapoport apparatus during aluminum electrolysis [5]. It has been proved that the FGM cathode showed better resistance to sodium expansion and penetration than the simple TiB2/C composite cathode. 

On the other hand, electrical resistance of cathode materials is an importance performance concerned to energy consumption in aluminum reduction cells. It has been found that the electrical resistance for carbon cathodes are influenced by materials, microstructures and

temperatures[6-8].The electrical resistances of carbon cathode with Tifh-coating have been reported, to decrease to some extent with TiB2 addition [9, 10]. 

In this investigation, electrical resistances of Tifh-C/C FGM cathode materials were measured in the temperature range of 25-960 °C in Ar atmosphere before and after aluminum electrolysis. And the microstructures of the tested FGM cathode samples were inspected using SEM. The aim of this work is to explore the effects of microstructure of Tifh-C/C FG

M cathode on its electrical resistance in connection with elevated temperature and electrolysis process. ###### **Experimental** ###### FGM Cathode Samples Preparation In this work, two samples had been prepared for comparison. In general, the electrical resistivity of both TGI and TG2 samples first increased and then decreased in the whole range of test temperatures. As the temperature increases during the measurement is close to that as high as in anode baking, the cathode samples could be like 193 undergoing a secondary heat-treatment. It is noticed that TG2 sample demonstrates all lower resistivity than TGI that even shows an second increase in resistivity after 750°C. This could be due to the gradient layer in TG2 impairing the distinct difference in thermal expansion between Tifh-rich function layer and the carbon base that again reduce its inner resistance. In contract, the absence of the gradient layer in the simple composite cathode sample (TGI) would result in a higher inner resistance in elevated temperatures, since the micro-cracks in the TiB2-layer and the carbon base may cause poor thermal stability and higher inner stress. ###### Electrical Resistivity after Aluminum Electrolysis Figure 3 and Figure 4 showed the electrical resistivity change of TGI and TG2 after aluminum electrolysis, compared with the corresponding values before electrolysis. It is seen that the electrical resistivity after electrolysis increases distinctly for sample TGI, while increases only some extent for TG2. In connection with the results of sodium expansion for both samples [5], it is considered as a result of cryolite/sodium penetration. During aluminum electrolysis, the cryolite/sodium penetration deteriorates the materials of samples, which induces cubical dilatation and micro-cracks within the samples, so that their electrical resistances increase after electrolysis. ###### SEM Characterization 

The microstructures of the cathode samples before aluminum electrolysis were examined by SEM, as shown in Figure 5. It indicated that the Tifh-rich layer had the least internal porosity about 8.37% (obtained by image analysis), the carbon base had the highest internal porosity, 25.20%, and the gradient layer was in middle with 15.85%. **1.** At elevated temperatures (350 -960°C), the electrical resistivity of T1B2-C/C FGM cathode sample is 33.86-27.04 ufl-m, lower than that of the cathode sample without FGM layer.

Xin Qiu , Bing Xie* , Lu Jiang , Xie Zhang , Jiang Diao , Hong-Yi Li

###### **Abstract** 

Duplex converter process, in which the first converter is used for removing phosphorus from hot metal (De-P), is an important way to produce low P-content and ultra-low P-content steels. In order to improve phosphorization removal and formation of slag with high basicity at relatively low temperature during dephosphorization converter process, effects of temperature, silicon content in hot metal and varied compositions of the De-P converter slag on phosphorus distribution between the slag and hot metal were investigated with thermodynamic calculations and by laboratory scale experiments in present work. Results showed that phosphorus distribution ratio between slag and metal was varied in 10.6-26.6 when basicity of the slag was in the range of 1.5-2.1 at 1370H, and the distribution ratio was increased with increasing basicity and FetO content in the slag. 

###### **Introduction** 

It is known that phosphorus exists in steel in the form of solid solution, which can significantly improve strength and hardness of steel at room temperature. However, the plasticity and toughness of steel, especially the low temperature plasticity is sharply reduced and leads to high ductile-brittle transition temperature. This phenomenon is commonly known as cold brittleness of steel [1-3]. Hence, phosphorus should be removed as much as possible in the steelmaking process, because it is generally harmful to the iron and steel products. 

So far, there are mainly three processes for dephosphorization, including pretreatment the hot metal, secondary refining and duplex converter process [4]. The duplex steelmaking process that originated in Japan has been proven to be an effective way to treat phosphorus in hot metal [5]. In general, the duplex steelmaking process is characterised by treating the hot metal with two LD converters (i.e. one for dephosphorization and the other for decarburization). The duplex steelmaking process adopted by the metallurgical engineers in some country is mainly focused on the 

199 

production of ultra-lo

w phosphorus steel. Although the duplex converter process has been used in steelmaking process fundamental research on the dephosphorization process has seldom been conducted and reported. According to this background, this work attempts to investigate kinds of factors, including content of silicon in hot metal, basicity and FeO content in final slag, on dephosphorization in the duplex dephosphorization converter. The value of Lp increased with increasing FeO under the experimental conditions (Figure 5) and which was in accordance with the data reported by Lee et al. [12]. The FeO played the role of the oxygen potential, phosphorus in hot metal was oxidized by FeO in slag to P2O5. ###### **Conclusions** 

1. The value of Lp gradually increased with increased of the final slag basicity when the basicity was in the range of 1.5-2.1. The value of Lp reached 26.6 when the basicity was 2.1. 

2. The value of Lp increased with increasing of mass percentage of FeO in final slag. The FeO content would be controlled about 25%, which was favorable to dephosphorization. 

3. The dephosphorization ratio increased with increasing Si content in hot metal, but the effect was not noticeable when Silicon content was more than 0.4%. When Silicon content in hot metal was less than 0.2%, the dephosphorization ratio would be slightly decreased, because the slag was short of enough the free CaO on dephosphorization. Therefore, silicon content in hot metal should be controlled between 0.2% and 0.4%.

###### **Abstract** 

This research was conducted to study the changes of microstructure, chemical composition and mechanical properties of IN718 superalloy after adding aluminum to the ESR process slag. The experiments were performed in VIM and ESR furnaces. The results showed adding 1.5 percent aluminum to the slag increase lave phase in the IN718 samples from 0.34 percent in the base sample to 3.0 percent. It also indicated that the more increase of aluminum in slag cause decrease in the aluminum absorb yield in the superalloy.it is observed that increasing aluminum from 0.7 to 1.1 and then to 1.5 percent caused a decrease of absorb from 91.4 to 76.3 and 74.6 percent respectively due to increasing of aluminum oxidation. According to the results, tensile strength increased and ductility declined in the IN718 samples mainly because of rising the amount of y' volume fraction. 

###### **Introduction** 

IN718 superalloy is an iron- nickel base superalloy with constant mechanical properties at medium at high temperatures. For the past seven years a considerable amount of time and effort has been expended by both suppliers and users in the study of Alloy 718 [1]. The interest in this material stems not only from the interesting metallurgy associated with the alloy, but with the large usage of the material in

numerous applications In fact many people believe that the projected use of this alloy increase significantly over the next several years, The large use of Alloy 718 is the result of its performance in respect to high strength, good ductility, good repair weld ability and from its versatility of being supplied in various product forms. This superalloy is used in wide ranges of industries such as aerospace and gas turbines [2]. In the past more than 20 years many researchers did a lot of work to improve the structure stability of IN718 at high temperatures and intended to develop a new 718 type alloy to be used beyond 650 °C. One of the methods is to control and phase precipitation behavior by means of adjustment of Al, Ti and Nb contents. The other idea is to strengthen the matrix by altering the content of solid solution elements such as W and Co. The adjustment of these alloying elements can change phase 

207 

precipitation behavior [3]. If detailed information dealing with phase precipitation behavior can be obtained before experimental work for alloy development, a lot of time can be saved and the development cost can also be reduced. In recent years, computer modeling based on experimental data plays an increasing role in alloy design and development. Adding Al to the Iron and Nickel increas the strength of superalloy by formation of y phase and subsequence formation of T| phase. Ti in IN718 superalloy also helps the formation of MC carbides and gamma prime phase. Increasing Al/Ti and (Al + Ti)/Nb will lead to form finer particles of _Y ._ More uniform distribution of the precipitates and enhancing stability off in IN718 superalloy [4]. Adding Al to slag of ESR process can reduce the oxide inclusions because of the strong tendency of Al to oxidation. In addition, tensile properties of IN718 superalloy improve. The most significant inclusions in IN718 superalloy are AI2O3 and TiN that were found in agglomerate forms. Thermodynamic calculation results indicate that the effect of increasing Al shows a strong increase in solvus while phase solvus shows mildly decrease when Al level is less than 2%, after that it dramatically decreases [5]. Laves phase precipitation and the appearance of phase are occurred when Al content reaches 2%. In fact, when Al content is beyond 1.5%, phase has already precipitated in a considerable scale. Shows the fraction of increases greatly while the fraction of phase decreases remarkably with the increment of Al content. Based on thermodynamic theory, if these particles were not existed in the melt during cooling agglomeration would not accrue and the superalloy will be cleaned By adding Aluminum to the slag, the metal reacts with oxygen to form oxide inclusions [6]. In this research the effect of adding aluminum to slag of ESR process on chemical composition, microstructure and mechanical properties of IN718 superalloy is investigated.

Mehmet Bugdayci, Murat Alkan, Onuralp Yiicel

Keywords: Metallothermic process, Mill-scale, Fe-based alloys 

###### Abstract 

In this study, iron based alloys (Fe-Mo, Fe-Cr-Ni, etc.) were produced by using aluminothermic methods starting from Mill Scales obtained continuous casting processes. Mill scales are an oxidised layer of steel alloys containing

iron oxide, which includes +2, +3 values, on the surface of slabs and billets occurring during annealing in heating furnace at integrated iron and steel milling plant, and continuous casting unit. In the metallothermic experiments, different ratios of starting mixtures and addition of the oxide powders (AI2O3, SiC>2, CaO, MgO) were examined, and their effects on the metal recovery and alloy compositions were carried out. The samples were characterized by using chemical analysis (AAS), XRD, XRF and SEM/EDS techniques. 

###### Introduction 

Self Propagating High Temperature Synthesis process (SHS) has many favour compared to the furnace applications, such as low energy requirement, low cost, very short processing time and simple operation, [1, 2]. In a SHS process, the ignition starts the combustion and propagates throughout the reactant mixture yielding the desired product. However, the disadvantages of the process such as inhomogeneous or unreacted products due to undesirable reaction rates needs to be overcome by changing some parameters such as ignition temperature, particle size, additive, atmosphere etc. [3, 4]. Mill scale is a layer of iron oxide which forms on ferrous materials cooling after being processed in hot rolling or continuous casting plants. Mill scale contains iron (II) and iron (III) oxides, which result in a 70% total iron content in oxide form. Not being able to reuse this material will prevent the raw material entering the production plant from being fully utilized [5]. This study aimed to produce Fe-based alloys via SHS (Self Propagating High Temperature Synthesis) metallurgy which is attractive process technique regarding fast and low-cost production ability of cast alloys by using high metallic iron content by reducing continuous casting mill scale.

###### **Abstract** 

CSP thin slab continuous casters are well used in recent years. The control of heat transfer in the mold is very important because it is correlated with several slab defects. The mean heat flux of CSP mold was studied based on the plant production data of LCAK steel and weathering steel. The effect of various operation conditions on the heat flux was analyzed and discussed. The results showed that the heat flux was 2.1-2.6 MW/m<sup>2</sup> on the wide face and 1.2-2.2 MW/m<sup>2</sup> on the narrow face for the casting of LCAK steels. During the casting of weathering steel, the heat flus was mostly 2.05-2.5 MW/m<sup>2</sup> on the wide face and was 1.1-1.8 MW/m<sup>2</sup> on the narrow face. The heat flux depended largely on the casting speed. The heat flux on the wide face increased obviously with increasing casting speed when the casting speed was relatively low; however, at high speed, the heat flux increased slowly or kept constant. At low casting speed, the heat flux depended little on the superheat of the molten steel. The mean heat flux depended little on the level fluctuation at continuous casting mold. 

###### **Introduction** 

CSP thin slab continuous casters are used more frequently in recent years for its low cost of construction and manufacturing. The structure of CSP mold is very different from that of conventional thick slab casting mold, inducing the difference of heat flux between them. There have been some studies about the heat flux of thick and medium slab casters [1, 2]. Heat transfer in the mold is very important for the solidification of molten steel because it is correlated with several slab defects such as slab break-out, longitudinal crack, and surface depression. Moreover, higher casting speed is desired to improve the productivity. The control of solidified shell is extremely important. The heat flux is largely influenced by several casting parameters such as the cooling intensity of the mold, the casting speed[3], the mold flux powder [3, 4] and the carbon content of steel as well [5]. The investigation on the heat flux and affecting parameters can help to understand the solidification of molten steel in the mold. 

In the current work, the characteristics of the mean heat flux at four faces of a CSP continuous casting mold at steady casting stage were studied based on the plant production data of low carbon Al killed (LCAK) steel and weathering steel (WS). The effect of various operation parameters, including casting speed, superheat in tundish and surface level fluctuation at the mold on the heat flux

was analyzed and discussed. 227 The Mean Heat Flux of the Continuous Casting Mold Heat flux is described as the ability of exporting the heat released by steel solidification on the entire face of copper plates of the mold. The mean heat flux of wide faces was almost in the ranee of 2.1-2.6 MW/m2 while that of narrow faces was in the ranee of 1.2-2.2 MW/m2 when LCAK steel was casted. For weathering steel, the mean heat flux of wide face was mostly in the range of 2.05-2.5 MW/m2 and was 1.11.8 MW/m2 m the narrow face. It is expected that the heat fluxes at two broad faces or two narrow faces should be equal or very close. However, as shown in Figures 2 and 3, on the wide face, the actual heat flux of fixed side was larger than that of loose side. The deviation value of LCAK steel and weathering ste

el were approximately 0.05 MW/m and 0.07 MW/m respectively. On the narrow face, when the heat flux was < 1.7 MW/m for LCAK steel or 1.5 MW/m for weathering steel, the heat fluxes on the two narrow faces were almost equal. However, when the heat fluxes were >1.7 MW/m , the heat flux of right side was larger than that of left side. Figure 2. Comparison of the heat flux of different faces of the mold when LCAK steel was casted: (a) wide face; (b) narrow face Figure 3. Comparison of the heat flux of different faces of the mold when weathering steel was casted: (a) wide face; (b) narrow face The asymmetric feature of the heat flux may be induced by several factors, such as the taper of mold, the thickness of copperplate, the wear of copperplate, the thickness of coating [6], and the centering of submerged entry nozzle (SEN). Since there was no taper on the wide face and the industrial data was over three months, the first three factors listed above were not the main reasons for the asymmetric feature. The most possible reason was the asymmetric thickness of 229 coating on the two sides of wide face and the mis-centering of SEN. Especially because the CSP mold is very thin, a small deviation of SEN from the center in the thickness direction would cause great difference on the heat flux of the two sides of wide face. Furthermore, the drift of flow stream would appear, inducing thinner solidified shell on the side with larger stream, then the thinner shell will contact with the copper plate closer under the action of static pressure of the molten steel. The drifted stream moves a shorter distance to the wide face, and keeps a higher temperature when reaching the surface. The influence of SEN miscentering on the heat flux will be more apparent at higher casting speed, especially for the narrow faces of mold, this is why the asymmetric phenomenon existed on the narrow faces when the heat flux was larger than the critical value. The effect of various operation parameters on the heat flux was analyzed and discussed. The following conclusions were derived: - (1) The mean heat flux was 2.1-2.6 MW/m2 on the wide face and 1.2-2.2 MW/m2 on the narrow face when LCAK steel was casted. During the casting of weathering steel, that on the wide face was mostly 2.05-2.5 MW/m2 and was 1.1-1.8 MW/m2 on the narrow face; - (2) Th

e mean heat flux, especially on the wide face, was asymmetric, which may be caused by the asymmetric thickness of coating on the two sides of wide face and the mis-centering of SEN; 

- (3) The heat flux of wide face increased obviously with increasing casting speed when the speed was relatively low, however, at high speed, >3.9 m/min for weathering steel for instance, the heat flux increased slowly or even kept constant. The casting speed had an influence on the heat flux of wide face more than that of narrow face; 

- (4) At low casting speed, the heat flux depended little on the superheat of molten steel, at high casting speed, for example 5.0 m/min of LCAK steel, the heat flux of wide face increased slightly as the casting speed increased; 

- (5) The mean heat flux depended little on the mold level fluctuation.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Modern engineering materials are required to be light weight and corrosion resistant,coupled with high strength and hardness.In this work,Al formed the parent metal and alloyed with 2.03% of Copper by sand casting process. The cast product 2024 was warm worked at various temperatures ranging from 300 to 560Oc at 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% deformation respectively and aged accordingly.The results showed that the mechanical properties vis-а-vis hardness, tensile improved with increasing % deformation at a higher temperature. This was due to the progressive close-up of the voids emanated from casting by increasing deformation which is evident from the micrographs. MATLAB was also adopted to generate a model capable of determining the trend of flow of stress at operating temperatures.This was of immense value due to an increasing impact at higher percentage deformation with temperatures.Hence, Al -alloys will find applications in land vehicles, ships, trains, and aircraft, at elevated temperature. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The problem of safe vehicle design with maximum impact energy absorption is a significant subject in structural crash worthiness design [1]. All engineering designs are expected to ensure the safety of users' life. This informed several studies meant to probe the causes of component failures in equipment, vehicles, and aerospace design and decide on appropriate solutions through materials selection techniques. A common example is in the design of crankcases and heads, piston, and cylinder blocks. As with engine blocks, cylinder heads can be made of Cast Iron or Aluminium Alloy. A head made of Aluminium alloy is lighter in weight than if it were made of Cast iron [2]. 

In this work, the quest is to study the influence of thermo mechanical ageing on Aluminium alloy in which Aluminium is the principal element (parent metal) with traces of other elements such as Copper, Magnesium, Iron, and Zinc. Aluminum is subject to internal stresses and strains when it is overheated; the tendency of the metal to creep under these stresses tends to result in delayed distortions. The warping or cracking of overheated Aluminium automobile cylinder heads is commonly observed [3]. Thus, the aerospace industry avoids heat altogether by joining parts with adhesives or mechanical fasteners. The

efficacy of Aluminum-Copper alloys lies in the inclusion of Copper in a range of 4-5% concentration. This formation of intermetallic phases together with the temperature-dependency of copper's solubility is the reason for Al-Cu being heat treatable. 

The general requirement for precipitation strengthening of supersaturated solid solutions involves the formation of finely dispersed precipitates during aging heat treatment (which may inclu

de either natural aging or artificial aging [4]. The aging must be accomplished not only below the equilibrium solvus temperature, but below a meta-stable miscibility gap called the Guinier-Preston (GP) zone solvus line [5]. ###### Aim and Objectives The aim of the research is to develop a non-ferrous Aluminium alloy material locally, that is a capable of competing with ferrous materials in service. This could be achieved by: (i) Employing a suitable precipitation strengthening and age-hardening heat treatment process with specified parameters (time, temperature and furnace atmosphere). (ii) Studying the effect of overheating on solution-treated and quenched alloy on its microstructure and hardness. (iii) Examining the microstructures with relevance to, impact strength, tensile and yield strength. ###### Contribution to Knowledge The work had helped to discover Aluminum -Copper alloy as an alternative material where strengthweight ratio and corrosion resistance are the required properties. The introduction of a mathematical model- f(x) = PiX2 +P2X +P3 in form of MATLAB [6] threw light into the extent of percentage deformation in variation to temperature limit.
